title: HamQASBench: A Hamiltonian-Informed Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating Quantum Architecture Search
authors: Jiayang Niu, Akib Karim, Yan Wang, Jie Li, Ke Deng, Azadeh Alavi, Muhammad Usman, Yongli Ren
abstract: Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) automates the design of parameterized quantum circuits for variational quantum algorithms, yet existing benchmarks organize instances by molecular identity or qubit count -- criteria agnostic to Hamiltonian structure -- and rely solely on energy accuracy, which cannot detect structural failures such as over-parameterization on near-product ground states. We introduce HamQASBench, a Hamiltonian-informed diagnostic benchmark organizing 11 molecules into five structural tiers via fingerprints derived from the Pauli operator basis, computational basis representation, and ground-state entanglement. A post-hoc critical-structure extraction procedure identifies minimal circuits consistent with each tier's requirements, complementing energy-based evaluation with per-qubit entanglement analysis and pairwise state fidelity. Benchmarking five QAS methods across four paradigms reveals failure modes invisible to conventional metrics: over-parameterization in the minimalism regime, eigenstate commitment under degeneracy, a representation bottleneck in strongly correlated systems, topology-induced routing failure, and circuit search space growth as a scalability bottleneck.
summary: This paper introduces HamQASBench, a novel benchmark that evaluates Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) by incorporating detailed structural information derived from molecular Hamiltonians. By organizing test cases into five distinct structural tiers—ranging from simple product states to highly correlated systems—it reveals failure modes in current QAS methods that are invisible when only energy accuracy is considered.
main_problem: Existing benchmarks for Quantum Architecture Search (QAS) are insufficient because they ignore the underlying structural properties of the Hamiltonian, leading to failure modes undetectable by energy accuracy alone.
main_result: The proposed HamQASBench organizes molecules into five structural tiers based on Hamiltonian fingerprints, revealing critical failure modes in QAS methods such as over-parameterization and representation bottlenecks.
method: The authors introduce a Hamiltonian-informed diagnostic benchmark that combines structural fingerprinting (from Pauli basis, computational basis, entanglement) with post-hoc critical-structure extraction procedures.
model_or_system: The study focuses on simulating molecular electronic structure using Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs), specifically analyzing the qubit Hamiltonians derived from molecules like BeH2 and H4 chains.
key_observables: Structural fingerprints ($r_Z, G_1, G_2$), per-qubit von Neumann entropy ($	ext{MAES}$), pairwise state fidelity ($F_{ij}$), training-evaluation gap, and redundancy ratio ($ho$).
important_parameters: Five structural tiers (Minimalism, Degeneracy, Representation, Topology, Scalability) define the test regimes; chemical accuracy is targeted at $1.6 	ext{ mHa}$.
main_assumptions: Energy accuracy alone is insufficient for diagnosing structural appropriateness; structural consistency metrics ($	ext{MAES}, F_{ij}$) are necessary to validate learned circuit structures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate Hamiltonian structural fingerprints and show how performance degrades when connectivity constraints (topology) are imposed, decoupling structural fidelity from energy metrics.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the shortcomings of current QAS benchmarks. It then details HamQASBench by defining its five structural tiers based on comprehensive Hamiltonian analysis. Finally, it benchmarks several QAS methods across these tiers, analyzing failure modes like over-parameterization and scalability limits.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous framework for testing quantum algorithms beyond simple energy minimization, forcing the evaluation of circuit structure relative to physical constraints, which is crucial for hardware-efficient algorithm design.
